title: “Mate-value backlash” may help explain anti-feminist attitudes among some Trump-era men, researchers say me-trump-era-men-researchers-say/
author: Eric W. Dolan
summary: Eric Dolan summarizes a Political Research Quarterly study by Stan Oklobdzija and Christopher Witko proposing that never-married men without a college degree show rising anti-feminist attitudes because of romantic and economic insecurity, which they call mate-value backlash. Using American National Election Studies data, they find that from 1970 to 2012 such men were not distinctively hostile to feminists, but in 2020 and 2024 they rated feminists about 10 points lower than college-educated never-married men. That hostility strongly predicted voting for Donald Trump even after controlling for party. The authors argue women's economic gains leave non-college men facing tougher competition in jobs and dating. Outside psychologist Rachael Robnett cautions that the data are correlational, that the term feminist is politicized and that women were not surveyed, so the explanation should be tested further.
points: The authors argue the anti-feminism of unmarried non-college men reflects romantic and economic insecurity rather than simple attachment to traditional gender roles.
The pattern is recent: before 2016 these men were not distinctively more hostile, but by 2020 and 2024 they rated feminists about 10 points lower.
Hostility toward feminists strongly predicted Trump voting in 2016, 2020 and 2024 even after controlling for party identification.
Robnett warns the data are correlational, the wording of the survey question changed over decades and women were excluded.
The article links the finding to manosphere communities and suggests future work on online amplification.
quotes: The authors argue this reflects a reaction rooted in romantic and economic insecurity, which they call “mate-value backlash,” rather than simply a desire to return to traditional gender roles.

Men who lack a college degree now face steeper competition in both the job market and the dating pool. This perceived loss of status and romantic insecurity, the authors suggest, generates resentment toward feminism and women’s equality.
However, during this 42-year stretch, never-married men without a college education did not generally show higher levels of anti-feminist hostility than other men.
Specifically, these men rated feminists about 10 points lower on the 100-point scale.
Additionally, this hostility toward feminists strongly predicted voting for Donald Trump among men overall in 2016, 2020, and 2024, even after controlling for party identification.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. Because the data is correlational, it cannot prove cause and effect.
An important caveat to the findings and their interpretation is that this research focuses exclusively on men,” Robnett explained.
This possibility is theoretically tenable, but should be directly tested through a study that includes both women and men before we can draw strong conclusions.
